To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the beam self‐field can create a plasma in the gas and the plasma can be used to accelerate the beam.
the beam self‐fields can create plasma and change the wakefield structure.
the plasma is created in the beam path by the beam itself.
In summary, our research is concerned with
modeling of E164X experiment.
modeling of the experiments, which will help us to understand the physics of plasma‐based accelerators.
modeling of plasma‐based accelerators and the interaction between the plasma and the beam, which is a very complicated process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the E164X experiment will provide an excellent opportunity to test the physics of plasma wakefields in the regime of intense bunches.
the E164X experiment will provide the most detailed and accurate information on the plasma wake‐field physics in the regime of very short bunches.
the plasma‐based accelerator is a promising candidate for the future high‐intensity electron accelerators.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the self‐fields of bunches can tunnel gas molecules and create the plasma, but the plasma formation time is longer than the bunch length and the plasma density is lower than the critical density, so that the bunch can still drive the plasma wakes and achieve very high accelerating gradient.
the plasma wakefields are not significantly affected by the ionization.
the beam‐driven plasma wake is not significantly affected by the gas‐ionization process in the case of the E‐164X experiment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
for a given beam energy, the beam current and gas pressure should be chosen to achieve the highest possible plasma density.
for the E164X experiment, the plasma density profile should be optimized to achieve the best performance of plasma wakefield acceleration.

the bunches with the charge per unit length of about 10–100μC/m and length of 100–200 μm will be able to tunnel ionize neutral hydrogen gas and create the plasma with density of 1017–1018 cm−3 in the experiment.
